opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the value of user data today is much lower than people imagined, at least compared with the internet era.

In the internet era, a recommendation system works because the user's behavior directly becomes the training signal. You click or you don't click, you stay or you leave, and that feeds straight back into the model. The loop is very short and the signal is very clean. So more users means better recommendations, which brings more users. That's the classic flywheel.

With large models it's different. Most of a model's capability comes from pre-training on huge amounts of data and from the compute you put in, not from the interactions users have with the product. A user chatting with a model doesn't naturally produce a high-quality label. Was the answer good? Often the user doesn't tell you, and even when they give a thumbs up or down, the signal is sparse and noisy. It's hard to turn that into something that meaningfully improves the base model.

There's also a question of where the bottleneck is. Right now the upper limit of the product is mostly determined by the upper limit of the model. If your model gets a generation better, the user experience jumps a lot, much more than you'd get from fine-tuning on user feedback. So the most important variable is still the model's intelligence itself, and that comes from scaling, better algorithms, and better data. Not mainly from usage data.

That doesn't mean the flywheel will never exist. I think it will appear once we find the right way to extract signal from interaction, for example with reinforcement learning, where the model can learn from outcomes in real tasks. If a model is doing long, multi-step work for you and you can tell whether the task succeeded, that's a much richer signal than a click. When that loop becomes efficient, user data starts to really matter again. But we're still at a fairly early stage of that. So for now, the more honest view is that the model is the product, and improving the model is the main thing.

r001.rationale: The response says model improvements from scaling and compute have a much larger effect than fine-tuning on user feedback, partly explaining why usage has not created a flywheel.

r002.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning as a possible future approach but does not identify on-policy training or say RL scales more efficiently than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It describes user feedback as sparse and noisy, but does not identify noise in external-environment feedback as an obstacle.

r004.rationale: The response contrasts clean recommendation signals with noisy model interaction signals, but does not say large-model learning is more sensitive to noise than recommendation systems.

r005.rationale: It suggests learning from outcomes in real tasks, where success can be assessed, as a richer interaction signal than clicks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most AI products today simply haven't reached the stage where usage data can actually change the model. For a flywheel to exist, you need a closed loop: users interact with the product, the interaction produces signal, that signal makes the model better, and the better model attracts more users. Right now that loop is broken in at least two places.

The first place it breaks is at the model layer. Most of the improvement in these systems still comes from pre-training, which is driven by compute and large-scale data from the internet, not from the few million conversations a product collects. If I have ten times more users next month, my base model doesn't get noticeably smarter. That is very different from a search engine or a recommendation system, where every click directly feeds back into ranking. So the thing people call "data" in AI products is not yet the thing that drives the core capability.

The second place it breaks is the quality of the signal itself. A thumbs up or thumbs down on a chat response is very thin. It tells you a user was satisfied or not, but it doesn't tell you much about why, and it doesn't naturally translate into a training objective. The signals that really matter for improving a model are things like task completion, whether the user actually used the output, whether they came back and corrected it. Most products haven't been designed to capture that, because they were built as demos of the model rather than as environments for learning.

There is also a more structural reason. The model layer and the application layer are often owned by different companies. The application has the users and the data, but it doesn't train the model. The model company trains the model, but it doesn't see the fine-grained product context. So even when data exists, it doesn't flow to the place where it could be used. The companies that can close this loop are those that own both ends, which is one reason I believe model and product have to be built together.

I'd add that the current paradigm is still early. As more of the improvement shifts from pre-training to post-training, to reinforcement learning on real tasks, the value of real user interactions goes up a lot. At that point the flywheel becomes possible, because what you collect from users starts to look like the thing you actually train on. So I don't think the absence of a flywheel is a permanent feature of AI products. It's a sign that we're still at the stage where scale of compute matters more than scale of users, and that will change.

r001.rationale: The response says compute matters more than user scale and that pre-training drives most improvement, while product conversations do not noticeably improve the base model.

r002.rationale: It mentions future reinforcement learning on real tasks, but does not identify on-policy training or explain that it makes RL scale more efficiently than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It describes thin or low-quality product feedback, but does not identify noise in feedback from external environments as an obstacle.

r004.rationale: It contrasts AI chat feedback with search and recommendation clicks, but does not claim large models are more sensitive to noise.

r005.rationale: It names richer signals such as task completion and user corrections, but does not say that new interaction forms could reduce noise in collected feedback.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that collecting more user data doesn’t automatically make the model better. A data flywheel needs a complete loop: users interact with the product, those interactions provide useful feedback, and that feedback improves the product enough to attract more users.

With AI, the feedback part is difficult. If a user asks a question and gets an answer, we don’t necessarily know whether the answer was good. They might stop because they’re satisfied, or because they’ve given up. And for an open-ended task, even knowing which answer they prefer doesn’t always tell us whether it’s correct.

There’s also a gap between the data a product collects and the data that’s useful for training. A lot of interactions are repetitive; turning them into a reliable learning signal takes work. So usage can grow much faster than the model’s ability to learn from that usage.

I’d expect the flywheel to emerge first in tasks where outcomes are verifiable. If you can tell whether a piece of code passes its tests, for example, you have a much clearer signal. The key isn’t just having more users. It’s having a way to turn what happens during use into measurable improvement.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention compute scaling or compare its gains with alternative approaches.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss on-policy training or compare RL with pre-training.

r003.rationale: It describes uncertainty and difficulty in interpreting user feedback, but does not identify noise in feedback from the external environment.

r004.rationale: It does not compare large-model learning sensitivity to noise with traditional recommendation systems.

r005.rationale: It points to verifiable tasks as having clearer signals, but does not suggest new forms of interaction to reduce feedback noise.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that more usage doesn’t automatically mean better training data. A product can have millions of conversations, but it’s often unclear which responses were actually good. If a user stops chatting, did we solve their problem, or did they give up? That’s a very weak feedback signal.

And even when you have useful feedback, turning it into a better model isn’t straightforward. You need to identify what the model should have done differently, train on that signal, and make sure the improvement generalizes without hurting other capabilities. There are several steps between collecting data and improving the product.

So I think the flywheel will emerge first in tasks where the outcome is verifiable. With coding, for example, you can check whether the code runs and whether the tests pass. If you can connect user interactions to a reliable measure of success, then usage can generate better data, better data can improve the model, and the better model can attract more usage. The missing piece is often that reliable signal, rather than the volume of data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses weak feedback signals and the steps needed to improve a model, but does not mention larger gains from scaling compute.

r002.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement learning, on-policy training, or a comparison with pre-training.

r003.rationale: It describes ambiguous user-interaction outcomes as weak feedback and says the missing piece is often a reliable success signal, identifying noisy feedback as an obstacle to a flywheel.

r004.rationale: It does not compare large-model learning’s sensitivity to noise with traditional recommendation systems.

r005.rationale: It points to verifiable tasks and reliable success measures, but does not suggest that new forms of interaction could reduce noise.
